titleStmt.title: “The research is happening in the text fields” – Are Linked Open Data and Art History a good match?
titleStmt.author: Giacomo Nanni
Linda Freyberg
Sabine de Günther
Marian Dörk

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: “The research is happening in the text fields” – Are Linked Open Data and Art History a good match?

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: Where the boundary falls between what an art-historical research project can express as Linked Open Data and what it must leave as prose.
span.quote: A recurring question is: What should be modeled as linked open data (LOD) and what should be entered as free-form text?

span.label: Structured vocabularies buy accuracy and queryability - so what is lost when the reflexive, contextual part of humanities research is forced into them?
span.quote: Despite the proven utility of data standards, vocabularies, and authority files providing for accuracy, context, and unambiguity, there is also a need for an open space to formulate and present tentative observations.

span.label: Argues that only the quantitative, queryable part of art-historical research is worth modelling as triples, and bridges the rest to it through visual interfaces rather than forcing it into ontologies.
span.quote: With this contribution we present how we bridge LOD and full text descriptions through information visualization.

span.label: critique
span.quote: In terms of representing the research process it is not worth making this part machine -readable as a basis for formal queries.

span.label: linked open data modelling in art history
span.quote: A recurring question is: What should be modeled as linked open data (LOD) and what should be entered as free-form text?

span.label: practice-report
span.quote: We use Art History research, in particular, the project “Restaging Fashion - Digital contextualization of vestimentary sources” (Refa), as one example to show how emerging discourses within the research process can be mapped in a knowledge organization system and which aspects may not be formally represented.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: an ontology can never close: no cultural artefact is finally contextualisable, and the vocabularies are uneven across subtopics
span.quote: Complex ontologies will never be completely exhaustive since no cultural artifact or experience could be fully and finally contextualized and vocabularies are not equally accurate and detailed for every subtopic.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the target moves: meanings shift over the life of the project doing the modelling
span.quote: In addition, contexts and meanings shift over time, even during the timeframe of a research project.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the cost of manual tagging is what forces institutions to publish shallow metadata, which then constrains what anyone can ask of the data
span.quote: This leads institutions to publish only a subset of the available information, exposing minimal metadata (Doerr et al. 2010), which might prevent researchers from using the data and constrains them to conventional research methods.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: deep modelling is not durable either - the British Museum modelled its whole collection in CIDOC CRM and then could not keep it accessible
span.quote: The British Museum, on the other hand, structured its entire collection using CIDOC CRM, but was unable to preserve its database in a consistent and accessible manner (Lincoln, 2015).

span.label: One project, one discipline: the argument is illustrated by Restaging Fashion rather than tested across cases.
span.quote: As part of the Restaging Fashion project, we devised different experimental prototypes, linked specific parts of the textual description to artworks, to classification entries, to archival sources as well as to other cultural heritage objects

span.label: The boundary it proposes - quantitative to triples, reflexive to interfaces - is asserted rather than operationalised; nothing says where a given sentence falls.
span.quote: In particular quantitative information, for instance, on objects and their relations, which can be queried and expressed statistically, are worth to be modeled in triple structures.

span.label: Linked Data, reference ontologies and authority files, applied to art-historical research and found to fit only part of it
span.quote: In Digital Humanities (DH) research this process and its specific structure has to be represented on a data level.

span.label: linked open data
span.quote: The potential of these applications is obvious: LOD allows data to be reused and redistributed, revealing relationships with other data on the Web (Berners-Lee 2006).

span.label: CIDOC CRM
span.quote: Sophisticated ontologies like CIDOC CRM encourage the detailed description of an object through an event-driven structure, which makes it a very powerful tool for the cultural heritage sector by providing for the possibility of adding meaning to the original data.

span.label: free-form text
span.quote: A recurring question is: What should be modeled as linked open data (LOD) and what should be entered as free-form text?

span.label: information visualization
span.quote: With this contribution we present how we bridge LOD and full text descriptions through information visualization.

span.label: ontologies
span.quote: Complex ontologies will never be completely exhaustive since no cultural artifact or experience could be fully and finally contextualized and vocabularies are not equally accurate and detailed for every subtopic.

span.label: metadata
span.quote: This leads institutions to publish only a subset of the available information, exposing minimal metadata (Doerr et al. 2010), which might prevent researchers from using the data and constrains them to conventional research methods.

span.label: triple structures
span.quote: In particular quantitative information, for instance, on objects and their relations, which can be queried and expressed statistically, are worth to be modeled in triple structures.

span.label: representation - as machine-readable structure, whose point is that a formal query can be run over it
span.quote: In terms of representing the research process it is not worth making this part machine -readable as a basis for formal queries.

span.label: representation - as something another researcher can read and understand, which the paper argues needs no formalisation at all
span.quote: It is more important to present it in a way that is accessible and understandable to other researchers, which does not require this high level of formalization, because it would end up in overcomplicated queries.

span.label: the unrepresentable - material the paper holds cannot be captured by either, quoting Galloway
span.quote: According to Galloway "there are some things that are unrepresentable. And the computer is our guide into that realm" (2011: 91).

span.label: builds-on → Galloway (2011: 91) on the unrepresentable
span.quote: According to Galloway "there are some things that are unrepresentable. And the computer is our guide into that realm" (2011: 91).

span.label: builds-on → Daquino et al. (2022) on institutional uptake of LOD-native systems
span.quote: Since 2006, when the term Linked Data was coined (see Berners-Lee 2006), according to Daquinoet al."only a few pioneers have abandoned legacy cataloguing and archiving systems to fully embrace the Semantic Web paradigm and manage their catalogues through LOD-native management systems" (2022).

span.label: builds-on → Berners-Lee (2006) on Linked Data
span.quote: The potential of these applications is obvious: LOD allows data to be reused and redistributed, revealing relationships with other data on the Web (Berners-Lee 2006).

span.label: contradicts → the programme of modelling cultural heritage research exhaustively in formal ontologies
span.quote: In terms of representing the research process it is not worth making this part machine -readable as a basis for formal queries.

span.label: Linked Open Data —contrasted-with→ free-form text
span.quote: A recurring question is: What should be modeled as linked open data (LOD) and what should be entered as free-form text?

span.label: CIDOC CRM —is-a→ ontologies
span.quote: Sophisticated ontologies like CIDOC CRM encourage the detailed description of an object through an event-driven structure, which makes it a very powerful tool for the cultural heritage sector by providing for the possibility of adding meaning to the original data.

span.label: triple structures —part-of→ Linked Open Data
span.quote: In particular quantitative information, for instance, on objects and their relations, which can be queried and expressed statistically, are worth to be modeled in triple structures.

span.label: The central question of the paper is a boundary question: what becomes structured data and what stays prose.
span.quote: A recurring question is: What should be modeled as linked open data (LOD) and what should be entered as free-form text?

span.label: Standards buy accuracy and unambiguity, but research also needs room for observations that are not yet settled.
span.quote: Despite the proven utility of data standards, vocabularies, and authority files providing for accuracy, context, and unambiguity, there is also a need for an open space to formulate and present tentative observations.

span.label: Modelling a collection early forces a trade-off between standardisation and semantic accuracy.
span.quote: Semantic data modeling of a collection during an early stage of the research prompts a trade-off to be made between data standardization and semantic accuracy.

span.label: Even major museums publishing LOD share only shallow models of their objects.
span.quote: it appears that these museums only share relatively shallow data models for their artworks on the web

span.label: Even institutions with deep semantic models publish shallow ones in practice - and one that did model deeply lost the result.
span.quote: The British Museum, on the other hand, structured its entire collection using CIDOC CRM, but was unable to preserve its database in a consistent and accessible manner (Lincoln, 2015).

span.label: Manual tagging is precise but does not scale, and automatic tagging fails on inconsistent data - so neither route reaches existing collections.
span.quote: Manual tagging can be performed by domain experts in a very precise manner, but it cannot be performed manually to large volumes of already existing content due to the lack of resources (Simou et al. 2017) or may not be conducted automatically due to inconsistencies and/or the lack of standardization in the datasets.

span.label: The paper's boundary: quantitative relations belong in triples, reflexive and contextual material belongs in visual interfaces.
span.quote: Other, more elaborated, reflexive, or contextualized information may require different forms of representations like visual interfaces.

span.label: Free text is treated as the starting point for semantic contextualisation rather than as a residue to be tidied away.
span.quote: Instead of hiding the full text in unstructured note fields, we approach this as a starting point for the semantic contextualization of the research process.

span.label: reference models such as CIDOC CRM
span.term: reference models such as CIDOC CRM
span.quote: reference models like CIDOC CRM (2022) offer a precise structural vocabulary to describe cultural heritage objects and their relations

span.label: the LOD / free-text question
span.quote: A recurring question is: What should be modeled as linked open data (LOD) and what should be entered as free-form text?

span.label: CIDOC CRM as an event-driven description of objects
span.term: CIDOC CRM as an event-driven description of objects
span.quote: Sophisticated ontologies like CIDOC CRM encourage the detailed description of an object through an event-driven structure, which makes it a very powerful tool for the cultural heritage sector by providing for the possibility of adding meaning to the original data.

span.label: Linked Open Data, as reuse and redistribution
span.term: Linked Open Data, as reuse and redistribution
span.quote: The potential of these applications is obvious: LOD allows data to be reused and redistributed, revealing relationships with other data on the Web (Berners-Lee 2006).

span.label: the unrepresentable
span.quote: According to Galloway "there are some things that are unrepresentable. And the computer is our guide into that realm" (2011: 91).
